name: Azerbaijani
variety: Standard North Azerbaijani (Baku norm, Latin script). The JIPA illustration and the acoustic vowel study describe the Tabriz (Iranian) variety; statements taken from them are marked as such.
sources: Ghaffarvand Mokari, Payam & Werner, Stefan (2017). Azerbaijani. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 47(2), 207-212.
Ghaffarvand Mokari, Payam & Werner, Stefan (2016). An acoustic description of spectral and temporal characteristics of Azerbaijani vowels. Poznań Studies in Contemporary Linguistics 52(3), 503-518.
Schönig, Claus (1998). Azerbaijanian. In Lars Johanson & Éva Á. Csató (eds.), The Turkic Languages. Routledge.
Householder, Fred W. & Lotfi, Mansour (1965). Basic Course in Azerbaijani. Indiana University.
contrasts: nine vowel qualities, including the open front /æ/ (ə) against mid /e/ and open back /ɑ/
voiced versus voiceless aspirated stops and affricates
palatal stops /c ɟ/ (spelt k, g) versus velar /ɡ/ (spelt q) and /k/ (mostly in Russian loans)
velar fricatives /x/ and /ɣ/ (spelt x, ğ) as full consonants, unlike Turkish soft g
no phonemic vowel length; long vowels only in careful pronunciation of Arabic and Persian loans
allophony: /c/ (spelt k) is a fricative [ç] in the syllable coda, most clearly at the end of polysyllabic words (çörək [tʃœˈɾæç], səksən)
word-final /ɡ/ (spelt q) is [x] or [ɣ] (otaq [oˈtɑx]) and alternates with /ɣ/ before a vowel-initial suffix (otağı)
stops are devoiced in coda position (Tabriz data, Ghaffarvand Mokari & Werner 2017)
/l/ is velarised [ɫ] next to back vowels
the sequences /ov/ and /œv/ are pronounced as diphthongs [ou̯] and [œy̯] before a consonant or a pause (dovşan)
/tʃ dʒ/ are [ts dz] in Tabriz and several other dialects, not in the Baku standard
/ɣ/ does not occur word-initially in native words
phonotactics: native syllables are V, VC, CV, CVC; final clusters occur mainly in loans and a few native stems (dörd, qırx, xalq)
backness harmony throughout the native word; rounding harmony only in high suffix vowels
/o œ e/ occur mainly in first syllables of native words

stress.type: fixed final by default, with morphological and lexical exceptions
stress.rule: Stress falls on the last syllable; it moves to the syllable before unstressable elements (negative -mA, copular and personal predicate endings, the question particle) and to the first syllable in imperatives, vocatives and some adverbs.
stress.cues: not instrumentally studied for the standard variety in the sources used

rhythm.notes: Ghaffarvand Mokari & Werner (2016) report a relatively strong intrinsic duration effect (open vowels longer than close ones) for Tabriz speakers.

length.notes: No native vowel length; lengthening appears in conservative pronunciation of Arabic and Persian loans, sometimes replacing a lost glottal stop or ayn (məna). Geminates occur in numerals and loans (yeddi, səkkiz, əlli).

intonation.declarative: non-final phrases end in a rise, successive phrases step down, final fall
intonation.yes_no_question: usually marked by intonation alone: there is no final fall and the last phrase is higher in pitch than the others; the particle -mI is optional
intonation.wh_question: falls at the end like a statement, with prominence on the question word
intonation.continuation: rising pitch at the end of each non-final phrase
intonation.accent_shape: rise to a high on the final stressed syllable of the word
intonation.notes: Pattern as described for Tabriz speech by Ghaffarvand Mokari & Werner (2017); no instrumental study of the Baku standard was available to me.

problems: ğ is handled with the Turkish soft-g rules: it is dropped with lengthening after a vowel and a following identical vowel is swallowed (dağ gives [daː], ağac gives [aːdʒ], oğul gives [oːul]); Azerbaijani ğ is a fricative [ɣ]
every word-final ə of a polysyllabic word is marked unstressed, so nənə and küçə are stressed on the first syllable instead of the last
t between front vowels is turned into [ts] (iti gives [itsi], getir gives [ɟetsir]), which is not standard
p t k are the unaspirated base2 stops; Azerbaijani voiceless stops are aspirated
unstressable suffixes are not handled: gəlmədi and bilmirəm get final stress
ov and öv stay [ov] and [œv] instead of the diphthongs [ou̯] and [œy̯]
k is always palatal [c], also next to back vowels and in Russian loans (Bakı gives [bacɯ])
/ɾ/ is a trill except between vowels, and a schwa is inserted before word-final r after a consonant
good: all nine vowels are present, including æ, ɯ, œ and y
palatal stops for k and g, [ɡ] for q with final [x], final and preconsonantal k as [ç]
velarised l next to back vowels; vowel harmony follows from the spelling

notes: The voice is marked 'status testing' in eSpeak NG.
